item.research_question: How can the strength of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steel be enhanced without sacrificing ductility, thereby evading the long-standing strength–ductility trade-off dilemma?
item.material_system: FeMnC TWIP steel (23.84% Mn, 0.61% C, balanced Fe) with a low stacking fault energy of 15–30 m Jm−2
item.processing_route: Cylindrical samples were subjected to torsion (180° or 360°) at an angular loading rate of 0.05° s−1 to generate a gradient nanotwinned structure, followed by uniaxial tensile deformation at a strain rate of ~10−4 s−1
item.test_conditions: Torsion tests at 0.05° s−1; tensile tests at ~10−4 s−1; micro-hardness measured with 500 g load for 15 s; microstructure analyzed via SEM, EBSD, and TEM (200 kV)
key_findings: Yielding strength of the pre-torsioned TWIP steel was doubled to ~730 MPa (from ~300 MPa) with no reduction in ductility.
A gradient nanotwinned structure formed with twin density increasing from the center to the outermost region (r/R=1).
Twin thickness increased with radial distance, reaching tens of nanometers at the surface.
Subsequent tensile deformation activated secondary and tertiary twins, creating a hierarchical nanotwinned structure.
The hardening modulus remained high until sample failure, unlike traditional processing which reduces ductility.
Finite element simulations showed yielding strength follows a law of mixture, with the hard shell significantly raising the yield strength of the soft core.
Different twinning systems were activated during torsion (e.g., T2, T4) compared to subsequent tension (e.g., T5, T1).
Dislocation dissociation at twin boundaries avoided stress concentration, playing a crucial role in retaining ductility.
item.mechanism: The gradient hierarchical nanotwinned structure enhances strength through the hard shell/soft core effect and twin barriers, while ductility is retained because sequential torsion and tension activate different twinning systems, creating a 3D hierarchical network that distributes plasticity and prevents premature failure via localized necking.
item.limitations: The method relies on materials prone to deformation twinning (low stacking fault energy); applying the same pre-torsion to 6061 Aluminum alloy resulted in enhanced strength but reduced ductility due to the lack of a hierarchical nanotwin network.
item.future_work: Develop other methods to produce non-uniform shear strains in metals prone to deformation twinning to enhance material performance, potentially applicable to axially symmetric structural components like axles in machines and high-speed trains.
quotes: we find that the yielding strength of the material can be doubled at no reduction in ductility.
the pre-torsion resulted in mechanical twins whose density increases with radial distance from the centre
preferential twin systems during pre-torsion may give way to the activation of other twin systems during subsequent tension
